claims.text: The target alloy has an overall density below 6 g/cm3.
The initial alloy is in a non-equilibrium metastable state.
The initial alloy contains a supersaturated solid solution.
The initial alloy contains dispersed metastable phases.
Controlled aging will cause stable intermetallic compounds to nucleate and grow.
The annealing-induced intermetallic compounds may be Ti-rich or Mg-enriched.
Aging releases supersaturation from the initial alloy.
The precipitated intermetallic phases alter local elemental distributions at or near the surface.
The altered surface chemistry preferentially oxidizes elements with strong oxide-forming tendencies.
Preferential oxidation produces a dense, adherent, and more protective oxide layer.
The protective oxide layer slows aqueous corrosion.
The protective oxide layer slows high-temperature oxidation kinetics.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, aging will produce a more noble corrosion potential.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, aging will lower the corrosion current density.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, aging will reduce weight gain during high-temperature oxidation.
Aging can be controlled to induce the intended intermetallic precipitation without causing full transformation to equilibrium phases.
The magnitude of corrosion and oxidation improvements depends on alloy chemistry, processing variables, and intermetallic-phase distribution.

contradictions.description: The initial state permits rapidly solidified or mechanically alloyed material, whereas the baseline and experiment specify an as-cast state and the boundary specifically invokes rapid solidification. A mechanically alloyed initial material would not have the stated as-cast baseline, leaving the controlled comparison internally inconsistent for that allowed case.
